questions.stem: In argument, a rebuttal is:
options: a summary of the writer's own contention at the very end
an anecdote placed at the start of a text to hook readers
a response that challenges or refutes an opposing argument
an agreement with every single point the opposing side has made
questions.explanation: A rebuttal answers the other side by showing where its argument is weak or wrong. Agreeing with the other side's points would be a concession, not a rebuttal.

questions.stem: ‘Of course, no one wants to see local businesses struggle during construction. But a decade of gridlock would hurt them far more.’ In these sentences the writer:
options: presents neutral data on how long the construction will take
concedes a point before rebutting it, appearing fair-minded
abandons the contention and accepts the opposing view in full
attacks local business owners for being selfish and short-sighted
questions.explanation: The writer grants the opposing concern, then argues that inaction would be worse, which makes the case seem reasonable. The contention is kept, not abandoned.

questions.stem: Why might a writer place her strongest argument last?
options: because conventions require all evidence to follow the conclusion
to leave it freshest in readers' minds as they form a judgement
because the strongest argument in a text needs no supporting evidence
to hide it from readers who only skim the opening paragraphs
questions.explanation: Sequence is a persuasive choice, and ending strongly leaves a lasting impression. Hiding the best argument would defeat its purpose, and strong arguments still need support.

questions.stem: A speech spends its first half describing rising rents in vivid detail and its second half outlining a rent cap. This problem–solution structure mainly aims to:
options: prove that the proposed rent cap has already succeeded in other places
make the audience feel the problem's urgency so the solution seems necessary
present both sides of the debate about rent caps with exactly equal weight
delay the contention so that it can quietly be withdrawn if it is challenged
questions.explanation: Building the problem first primes the audience to welcome a solution. The speech argues for one side throughout, so it does not weigh both equally.

questions.stem: ‘Libraries are more than books. They are warm places for the lonely, free internet for job seekers and safe after-school spaces. Cutting their hours cuts a lifeline.’ Which is the best summary of this argument?
options: Library hours should not be cut, because libraries provide vital community services.
Libraries should stock far more books and provide fewer computers for the public.
Libraries are used only by lonely people and by job seekers looking for work.
Libraries should open longer so that children can stay later after school ends.
questions.explanation: The contention is that hours should not be cut, supported by the services libraries offer. Arguing to keep hours is not the same as arguing to extend them.

questions.stem: To support a claim about teenage mental health, which evidence would most strengthen the writer's credibility with a sceptical audience?
options: a quote from a celebrity who has spoken publicly about her own stress
a single comment from the writer's teenage cousin about school pressure
a poll of the writer's own social media followers on how stressed they feel
findings from a large national study by a university research centre
questions.explanation: A sceptical audience is most persuaded by large, independent and expert evidence. A celebrity, a cousin or the writer's own followers offer small or unrepresentative samples.

questions.stem: A writer states that crime in a suburb 'has doubled', but the figures show a rise from two incidents to four. This use of the statistic:
options: exaggerates the problem by hiding a very small base number
proves that there has been a dramatic rise in serious crime
presents a balanced picture of how safe the suburb really is
is an expert opinion that readers have no grounds to challenge
questions.explanation: 'Doubled' is accurate but sounds alarming because the real numbers are tiny. Analysing argument includes recognising how true figures can be framed to mislead.

questions.stem: ‘The minister cites a report showing the scheme works. That report was funded by the company running the scheme.’ The writer seeks to:
options: attack the minister's personal life and private character
present a personal anecdote about using the scheme himself
undermine the opposing evidence by questioning its independence
support the minister's claim with further, independent evidence
questions.explanation: Pointing out who funded the report invites readers to doubt its objectivity, weakening the minister's case. The writer targets the evidence, not the minister's private life.

questions.stem: ‘Either we lower the speed limit to 30 km/h, or we accept that children will die on our streets.’ This strategy:
options: relies on expert testimony to prove a link between speed and injury
uses a personal anecdote to make the issue of road safety feel immediate
presents only two options, framing any alternative as unthinkable
offers readers a balanced range of different policy choices to consider
questions.explanation: This is a false dilemma: it ignores other options, such as crossings or traffic calming, so rejecting the proposal seems to mean accepting deaths. No expert or anecdote is cited.

questions.stem: ‘Allow one apartment tower, and soon the whole foreshore will be a wall of concrete.’ This is best described as:
options: a statistic showing the current rate of development along the foreshore
a concession that some development on the foreshore is acceptable
an analogy comparing the foreshore to the developed coastline of another city
a slippery-slope argument predicting an escalating chain of consequences
questions.explanation: The writer claims one step will inevitably lead to the worst outcome, which is a slippery slope. Far from conceding anything, the writer opposes even one tower.

questions.stem: ‘For ninety years, the town's Easter fair has been held on the oval. Moving it to an industrial estate would break faith with every family who built it.’ This appeals mainly to:
options: tradition and community loyalty
financial self-interest
scientific and expert authority
fear for physical safety
questions.explanation: The long history and 'break faith' invoke loyalty to the past and to the community. Nothing is said about cost, experts or danger.

questions.stem: ‘Why should a family in Mildura pay more for electricity than one in Melbourne?’ This question appeals mainly to:
options: a sense of fairness and equal treatment
fear of physical danger
national pride and patriotism
trust in expert authority
questions.explanation: The question frames a price difference as unjust, appealing to readers' sense of fairness. It names no danger and no expert.

questions.stem: One article calls a welfare policy 'a safety net'; another calls the same policy 'a handout'. The different labels mainly:
options: show that both writers agree on the value of the policy
provide statistical evidence about how many people receive the policy
signal that both pieces were written for young children
position readers to see the policy as protective or as undeserved
questions.explanation: 'Safety net' suggests protection for people who fall, while 'handout' suggests something given to people who have not earned it. The same policy is framed in opposite ways by connotation.

questions.stem: A writer argues that a new dam will devastate farmers, describing their land as 'the food bowl that feeds a nation'. How do argument and language work together here?
options: the metaphor undercuts the argument by making the farmers seem greedy
the language is neutral, leaving the argument to rest on statistics alone
the metaphor shifts the argument away from farmers to city water users
the metaphor raises the stakes, so harm to farmers seems a national concern
questions.explanation: Calling the land a nation's 'food bowl' turns a local loss into everyone's loss, strengthening the argument about farmers. The study design asks how arguments and language complement each other in exactly this way.

questions.stem: ‘What a triumph: a $40 million stadium, and still no bus to get there.’ The writer uses irony mainly to:
options: concede that the stadium already serves public transport users well
mock the project's priorities by praising it in words that mean the opposite
sincerely celebrate the new stadium's success and its value to the town
explain how the stadium was funded in calm, neutral and factual terms
questions.explanation: 'What a triumph' is undercut by the missing bus, so the praise is ironic and the target is poor planning. Taken sincerely, the line would make no sense alongside its second half.

questions.stem: ‘This ruling will destroy every small business in the state overnight.’ This sentence is an example of:
options: hyperbole
understatement
concession
statistical evidence
questions.explanation: The claim exaggerates for effect: 'every' business 'overnight' is not meant literally. Understatement would do the opposite, playing the impact down.

questions.stem: A headline reads 'Council Caves to Developers'. The verb 'caves' positions readers to see the council as:
options: decisive and highly principled
neutral and following procedure
generous to the whole community
weak and giving in to pressure
questions.explanation: To 'cave' is to collapse under pressure, so the headline casts the council as spineless. A neutral verb such as 'approves' would carry no such judgement.

questions.stem: An article about a proposed waste incinerator includes a graph whose vertical axis starts at 95 rather than 0, making a small rise in emissions look steep. The graph:
options: exaggerates the change in order to heighten readers' alarm
presents the data in the most neutral way that is possible
shows readers that the emissions have fallen sharply over time
replaces any need for the article to state a written contention
questions.explanation: Cutting off the bottom of the axis magnifies a small difference, a common way visuals augment an argument. The rise is real but its size is distorted, so the presentation is not neutral.

questions.stem: An opinion piece arguing that a heritage pub should be saved runs beside a sepia photo of crowds at the pub decades ago. How does the image augment the argument?
options: its nostalgic feel links the building to a shared history readers should protect
it provides evidence that the pub's building is now structurally unsafe
it shows readers the pub as it looks today, empty, neglected and run-down
it counters the article's argument by showing how overcrowded the pub was
questions.explanation: The sepia tone and crowds evoke a valued communal past, supporting the case for preservation. The photo is of the past, so it cannot show the pub today.

questions.stem: A cartoon shows a giant smartphone looming over a tiny child at a dinner table, while the parents stare at their own screens. The cartoonist's main criticism is aimed at:
options: phone makers for producing devices that are far too large
schools that ban students from using phones during class
parents whose screen use crowds out family connection
children who demand their own phones at too young an age
questions.explanation: The parents are absorbed in their screens while the child is dwarfed and alone, so the criticism targets their behaviour. The child has no phone, so the cartoon is not about children demanding them.

questions.stem: An online article includes hyperlinks to government reports. The hyperlinks mainly:
options: reduce the writer's credibility by sending readers to other websites
replace the need for the article's own supporting arguments
let readers verify the claims, boosting the writer's credibility
make the article's argument impossible for anyone to dispute
questions.explanation: Links to sources show the writer's claims can be checked, a feature of digital texts that builds trust. Sources make an argument more credible, but they cannot make it indisputable.

questions.stem: On a newspaper page, a large pull quote repeats the line 'Our kids deserve better' from an opinion piece. The pull quote mainly:
options: identifies the writer's professional qualifications
draws skimming readers to the article's emotional core
provides the main statistics that support the argument
marks the start of the writer's rebuttal of opponents
questions.explanation: A pull quote enlarges a line so readers who only glance at the page still meet the key appeal. It repeats an emotive line, not data or credentials.

questions.stem: A campaign video shows slow-motion footage of a koala in a burnt forest, scored with a single piano line, before the narrator speaks. These elements mainly:
options: present neutral scientific footage for viewers to interpret for themselves
use gentle humour to soften the issue for an audience of young viewers
signal to viewers that the video is a balanced, factual news report
create sorrow that primes viewers to accept the narrator's call to action
questions.explanation: Slow motion and a sparse piano score build grief before any argument is made, positioning viewers to agree. Music chosen for mood signals persuasion, not neutral reporting.

questions.stem: In a recorded speech, the speaker stresses the word 'chose' in: 'They chose to ignore the warnings.' The stress mainly:
options: softens the criticism so the speech sounds conciliatory
turns the statement into a question for the audience
highlights deliberate negligence, sharpening the blame
suggests the warnings were ignored by honest accident
questions.explanation: Emphasising 'chose' insists the failure was intentional, which intensifies the accusation. It does the opposite of suggesting an accident.

questions.stem: A podcaster quickens her pace and raises her volume while listing failures, then drops to a slow, quiet line: 'And still, nothing changed.' The contrast in delivery:
options: builds momentum, then lands the final line with heavy disappointment
shows listeners that the podcaster has run out of arguments to make
signals that she approves of the outcomes of the policy she describes
creates a light, comic tone to bring the segment to a cheerful close
questions.explanation: The rising energy of the list makes the sudden quiet more striking, so the final line carries the weight. Pace and volume are being used to persuade, not to signal approval.

questions.stem: An editorial differs from an opinion column mainly because it:
options: presents the official view of the publication rather than of a named individual
must by convention give exactly equal space to both sides of the issue it discusses
is written by a member of the public rather than by a journalist
contains only facts and uses no persuasive language of any kind
questions.explanation: An editorial speaks for the newspaper or site as an institution and is usually unsigned. It is openly persuasive; a letter to the editor is the form written by a member of the public.

questions.stem: An article praising a new fast-food outlet is written by the chain's chief executive. Readers' reactions are likely to be affected because:
options: chief executives are not permitted by law to publish their own opinion pieces
the writer's senior position guarantees that the article's claims are accurate
readers have no way of finding out who wrote an article in a newspaper
the writer's vested interest may lead readers to doubt the article's objectivity
questions.explanation: The study design notes that an author's identity can affect an audience's reaction, and someone who profits from the outlet has an obvious bias. Seniority does not guarantee accuracy.

questions.stem: A piece calling for more funding for hospital emergency departments is written by a nurse with twenty years' experience. Her identity most likely:
options: makes readers dismiss her claims entirely because she is not a doctor
means the piece contains no persuasive language or emotional appeals
turns the piece into an objective scientific report rather than an argument
lends first-hand authority, so readers may trust her account of conditions
questions.explanation: Long experience on the ward makes her an informed witness, which strengthens her credibility. Her expertise does not make the piece neutral; it remains an argument.

questions.stem: An opinion piece arguing for stronger dog-control laws is published the day after a widely reported dog attack on a child. The timing most likely:
options: ensures that readers will take the piece as neutral reporting
prevents the writer from using any emotional appeals at all
lets the writer harness readers' heightened fear and sympathy
makes readers less receptive, since the issue is now settled
questions.explanation: The context in which a text appears shapes its reception, and a fresh tragedy makes readers more open to calls for action. Timing does not change the piece's genre into reporting.

questions.stem: A business magazine argues against a four-day working week, stressing lost productivity. A union newsletter argues for it, stressing workers' wellbeing. This mainly shows that:
options: both of the pieces must have been written by the same author
arguments about work cannot appeal to an audience's values
writers select arguments that appeal to the values of their intended audience
only one of the two pieces actually contains a contention on the working week
questions.explanation: Each publication's readers care about different things, and the arguments are chosen accordingly. Both pieces clearly have a contention, for and against.

questions.stem: A letter to the editor is addressed to the state premier but published in a newspaper. Its wider readership is most likely:
options: expected to reply privately to the writer by post or by email
invited to add public pressure on the premier by sharing the writer's view
excluded from the argument, since the letter is meant for the premier alone
given a neutral report of the government's position on the issue
questions.explanation: Publishing an open letter turns readers into a secondary audience whose agreement increases pressure on the addressee. If it were meant for the premier alone, it would not be published.

questions.stem: A speech to parliament on youth unemployment includes the line: 'To every young person listening tonight: you are not the problem.' This direct address mainly:
options: replaces the speech's argument with neutral background information
reaches a second audience, reassuring young people while pressing politicians
signals that the speech is meant only for young people and not for MPs
concedes that young people are to blame for their own unemployment
questions.explanation: Speaking past the chamber to young listeners widens the audience and implies the problem lies with policy makers. The line rejects blaming young people rather than conceding it.

questions.stem: Which sentence best rebuts an opposing view through respectful disagreement?
options: ‘My opponent clearly hasn't done any research at all before coming here tonight.’
‘I refuse to respond to that argument, because I find it far too offensive.’
‘My opponent rightly values safety, but the evidence shows the ban would not improve it.’
‘Only an idiot could seriously believe that a ban would ever improve anybody's safety.’
questions.explanation: Respectful disagreement acknowledges the opponent's values and then focuses on the argument and evidence. Insults and refusals to engage abandon the argument.

questions.stem: A student is preparing a point of view presentation on an issue that personally upsets her. According to the study design, effective persuasive texts:
options: rely on personal attacks on opponents to show how high the stakes are
focus on the arguments and temper personal responses to contentious issues
express anger freely and at length, since strong passion always persuades
avoid contentious issues altogether, so that no one in the room is challenged
questions.explanation: The study design describes effective persuasive texts as focusing on the arguments and tempering personal responses to powerful or contentious issues. Unchecked anger can alienate an audience.

questions.stem: While listening to a debate, which note best shows a student monitoring and evaluating an argument?
options: ‘Speaker 2 talked for about three minutes before sitting down.’
‘Speaker 2 spoke after speaker 1 and before speaker 3.’
‘Speaker 2: fines cut littering – cites one council only; is it typical?’
‘Speaker 2 sounded confident and wore a very smart jacket.’
questions.explanation: The note records the claim and its evidence and then questions whether the evidence generalises. Appearance, length and speaking order say nothing about the argument's strength.

questions.stem: In an analysis of argument, saying that a writer 'positions readers' means that the writer:
options: summarises both sides of the issue equally
addresses a single, named reader directly by letter or email
shapes how readers are invited to view the issue
states facts that readers are unable to dispute
questions.explanation: Positioning is the way an author's arguments, language and visuals encourage a particular view. It is about influence, not about undisputed facts or balance.

questions.stem: Which approach suits the body of an analysis of argument?
options: group the techniques alphabetically and give one example of each, without discussing any of their effects
summarise the text in full, then give your own view of the issue in the final paragraphs
list each technique in the order it appears, naming it without discussing its effect on readers
follow the argument's development, analysing how language and visuals position readers at each stage
questions.explanation: Tracing the argument as it unfolds shows how arguments and language work together over the text. Naming techniques without their effects is identification, not analysis.

questions.stem: Which sentence best analyses how argument and language interact?
options: The writer's main argument is that the plan is far too expensive for the council to afford.
I disagree with the writer, because I think the plan would actually save the council money.
By casting the plan as 'a gamble with our children's lungs', the writer turns a cost dispute into a moral one.
The writer uses a metaphor, 'a gamble with our children's lungs', which is a very persuasive technique.
questions.explanation: The sentence links a specific phrase to how it reshapes the argument for readers. Labelling a metaphor 'persuasive' without saying how is identification, not analysis.

questions.stem: A student analyses an article and its accompanying cartoon on the same issue. The strongest approach is to:
options: show how the cartoon reinforces or extends particular arguments in the article
analyse the cartoon only, since visual texts always persuade more than words do
discuss each text in a separate half of the response, with no links between them
describe the cartoonist's drawing style in close detail, without reference to the issue
questions.explanation: The study design stresses how visuals support and augment argument, so the analysis should connect the two texts. Treating them in isolation misses how they work together.

questions.stem: Two pieces on a curfew differ: one uses statistics and a measured tone, the other anecdote and outrage. In a comparative analysis, the most insightful point is that:
options: both pieces use exactly the same strategies to achieve exactly the same effect
each writer's approach suits a different audience and positions it differently
the measured piece is correct, because it relies on statistics rather than stories
the outraged piece is weaker, because emotional appeals never persuade anyone
questions.explanation: Comparative analysis explains how each text works on its audience, not which one is right. Emotional appeals can be highly persuasive, so dismissing them misreads the outraged piece.

questions.stem: Which structure is most effective for a point of view oral presentation?
options: a long list of facts, with the speaker's opinion revealed only in the very final sentence
a reading of a published article on the issue, followed by questions from the audience
a single anecdote, deliberately left without a contention so that listeners can decide
a hook, a clear contention, sequenced arguments with evidence, rebuttal, and a strong close
questions.explanation: A point of view text needs a clear position supported by ordered arguments and a response to the other side. Withholding a contention defeats the purpose of presenting a point of view.

questions.stem: In a spoken point of view text, why might a speaker restate her contention near the end?
options: to fill the remaining time once she has run out of arguments to make
repetition makes any speech sound more spontaneous and unrehearsed
listeners cannot reread, so repetition reinforces the key message
restating the contention is required by the formal rules of debating
questions.explanation: Spoken texts are heard once, so returning to the contention helps it stick. It is a choice that suits the spoken mode, not a formal requirement.
